record.original_question: Let M be the one-dimensional centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator. Is the derivative map f -> (M f)' continuous from W^{1,1}(R) to L^1(R)? In other words, whenever f_j converges to f in W^{1,1}(R), must the derivatives of the centered maximal functions converge in L^1(R) as well?

evidence.quote: Question 12. Is the map f 7→ (M f )′ continuous from W 1,1 (R) to L1 (R)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ denote the one-dimensional centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator, defined for $f\in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$ by
$$Mf(x) = \sup_{r>0} \frac{1}{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r} |f(y)|\,dy.$$
It is known that if $f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ then $Mf$ is weakly differentiable with $(Mf)'\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, so the map $T: f \mapsto (Mf)'$ is well-defined from $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ into $L^1(\mathbb{R})$.

Determine whether $T$ is continuous: that is, whether for every sequence $\{f_j\}\subset W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $f_j \to f$ in $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$, one has $(Mf_j)' \to (Mf)'$ in $L^1(\mathbb{R})$.
artifact.status_search_result: Cristian González-Riquelme (arXiv:2109.09691, 2021; published in J. Funct. Anal., 2023) proved that the map f ↦ (Mf)' is continuous from W^{1,1}(ℝ) to L^1(ℝ) for the one-dimensional centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator, resolving the question affirmatively.

status_evidence.title: Continuity for the one-dimensional centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator at the derivative level
status_evidence.snippet: We prove the continuity of the map f ↦ (Mf)' from W^{1,1}(ℝ) to L^1(ℝ), where M is the centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator.
status_evidence.claim: The continuity question is answered affirmatively.

status_evidence.snippet: Published version establishing continuity of f ↦ (Mf)' from W^{1,1}(ℝ) to L^1(ℝ).
